evidence_quotes.quote: Currently, CLTS is one of the most widely deployed behavioral hygiene and sanitation interventions [4]. Thirty-six countries have adopted CLTS as part of their national rural sanitation strategy and/or policy, including Burkina Faso [4,5]. CLTS is a behavioral and participatory approach that primarily relies on feelings of shame and disgust to mobilize rural communities to build toilets and end OD [6].

As a result, two organizations could be in the same geographic area (in the same municipality or in neighboring villages) deploying CLTS in different ways: one with a subsidy (full or partial) and one without. The communities in which the approach was deployed without subsidies generally refused to terminate OD by building the latrines at their own expense after learning that their neighbors had received subsidies under CLTS, even though they had different implementing actors.

evidence_quotes.quote: The institutional trigger is a meeting between the water and sanitation coordinating actors of the intervention zone and the key actors (village chiefs, notables, religious guides, etc.) of the targeted community.
These data came from household surveys, interviews with institutional and CLTS implementation actors, direct observations, and participation in CLTS processes.
The total score for an acceptance factor was thus proportional to the number of respondents who cited it during data collection.

Assessing the degree of acceptance of the social norms promoted by CLTS must go beyond a simple verbal commitment, such as “yes, we will commit to building latrines, to using them, to washing our hands with soap and water after using the latrines; we commit to stop practicing OD”.

criterion_notes.c1: Addresses rural household and community sanitation in Burkina Faso through Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) campaigns aimed at ending open defecation (OD) and motivating households to self-build and use latrines to achieve Open Defecation-Free (ODF) village certification (framed under SDG 6.2 sanitation access).
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES PLAIN WORDING (plain C2 = yes) BUT FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING (narrow C2 = no). Under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines institutional and governance factors: Section 3.1 ('Governance Factors', category score = 247) interviews ministry, regional/provincial, municipal, and NGO actors regarding institutional pre-triggering with village leaders, NGO-government coordination, national policy ambiguity between subsidized and unsubsidized CLTS implementation, and High Commissioner mediation for ODF certification, while Section 3.5.4 notes informal sanctions/fines threatened by village authorities against holdout households. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is 'no' because the intervention and determinants studied are behavioural promotion (CLTS social-norm promotion relying on shame/disgust and health awareness) and generic NGO/government project delivery and community mobilization, rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access. (Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, plain_criterion2_decision is 'exclude' because the paper also fails Criterion 4.)
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from 490 randomly sampled rural household surveys across 12 villages in three provinces plus 60 purposively sampled semi-structured interviews with national/decentralized officials, NGOs, health districts, municipalities, and community stakeholders (total N = 550), analyzed via content analysis and frequency scoring.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not measure or report an outcome relevant to sanitation access, connection, latrine coverage/ownership, latrine use, service availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. Village ODF status was used only as a sampling criterion for selecting study villages, and the sole empirical outcome reported (Table 4) is the frequency score of respondents citing each motivating factor as a reason for accepting/committing to CLTS behavioral social norms. In Section 4 (pp. 15-16), the authors explicitly acknowledge that verbal/written commitment to CLTS norms does not measure actual latrine construction or regular use.
criterion_notes.c5: Population and unit of analysis (490 rural households in 12 villages plus 60 institutional/community stakeholders in central-western Burkina Faso), exposure/determinants (CLTS triggering and perceived environmental, social, governance, territorial, and economic acceptance factors), outcome (citation scores for accepting CLTS social norms), and study design (cross-sectional survey and qualitative interview case study with content analysis) are clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

study_design: Cross-sectional mixed/qualitative case study using household surveys and semi-structured key-informant interviews analyzed via content analysis and frequency scoring
population_and_sample: 550 respondents in the central-western region of Burkina Faso (490 randomly selected adult household respondents across 12 triggered or ODF-certified rural villages in Sissili, Ziro, and Boulkiemdé provinces, plus 60 purposively selected central/decentralized government, NGO, health, municipal, and community stakeholders)
exposure: Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) behavioral hygiene/sanitation social-norm promotion and perceived environmental, social, governance/project-delivery, territorial, economic, and technological acceptance factors
outcome: Perceived acceptance of CLTS social norms, quantified as respondent citation frequency scores across 550 household and stakeholder interviewees for factors motivating commitment to CLTS norms (no household latrine access, ownership, construction, or usage rates reported)
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure), and additionally fails Criterion 4. The study investigates factors driving rural communities' social acceptance of behavioral hygiene and sanitation norms promoted by Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) in Burkina Faso. Under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, CLTS social-norm promotion and NGO/government campaign facilitation (institutional pre-triggering meetings, facilitator experience/language, natural leader buy-in, coordination across subsidized vs. unsubsidized NGO campaigns, and motivational visits by officials) constitute behavioural promotion and generic project delivery rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access. Furthermore, although the paper passes the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2 via its 'Governance factors' category, plain_criterion2_decision is also 'exclude' because Criterion 4 is not met: the study reports only respondent citation counts for perceived reasons to accept CLTS behavioral norms (Table 4) and does not measure household sanitation access, latrine ownership/use, availability, affordability, or exclusion.
